name: Wig powder (hair powder)

image.caption: Applying hair powder, circa 1750. Wellcome L0006483

lead: Hair powder was a fine starch-based powder, often scented with orange flower, lavender or orris root, that was applied to wigs and hair in 18th-century Europe. It gave the pale white or grey tone that signaled fashion and status, and it softened and unified the color of the hair.

The look came from the powder itself: a matte, uniform tone that hid greasy or uneven hair. It is documented in historical rather than clinical sources, and today it appears in costume, theatre and historical reenactment.

paras: Historically the powder was dusted or puffed over hair or a wig that had been stiffened with pomade, then brushed so the color looked even. Women usually aimed for grey or blue-grey; men for white. Costume wearers today use modern starch or cosmetic powders in similar ways.

Powdering was messy and inconvenient, and fine powder in the air is an irritant if inhaled. Historical powders sometimes had other ingredients, so modern costume use generally relies on cosmetic-safe products.

angle.text: Powder changed the color and finish of the hair itself, producing a uniform pale tone that was the period's mark of style. Today it is used for historical dress and costume looks.

lead: Hair powder, also called wig powder, is a fine powder made from ground starch, scented with orange flower, lavender or orris root, that was applied to wigs and to natural hair in 18th-century European fashion. It was usually off-white but sometimes tinted violet, blue, pink or yellow.[1]

It improved how someone looked by giving hair a pale, matte, uniform shade that signaled fashion and rank. Men powdered their wigs to white or off-white, while women typically powdered their own hair, with added pieces, to grey or blue-grey.[1]

Wig-wearing waned by 1765 except among groups such as coachmen and lawyers, revived in the 1770s Macaroni fashion, and by the 1780s young men were lightly powdering their own hair rather than wearing wigs. After 1790 powder remained mainly with older conservative men and women presented at court. In 1795 William Pitt the Younger imposed a tax of one guinea per year on hair powder, which the source says effectively ended the fashion.[1]
infobox: White, off-white; sometimes violet, blue, pink, yellow [1]

paras: Powder was finely ground starch, often scented. Colors besides white were produced for specific looks, and women's grey-blue tones differed from men's white.[1]

Powdered wigs became a mark of fashion in the 18th century. A naturally white horsehair wig eventually made powdering unnecessary for everyday court dress, though powdering was still seen as messy and inconvenient.[1] The 1795 tax under Pitt the Younger is credited by the source with ending the fashion for both wigs and powder.[1]
Costume makers, theatre professionals and reenactors apply powders to wigs to evoke period looks, and some modern hair-color and texturizing powders echo the idea of dusting hair for tone and finish.
